event.title: Ten years of CC Fest
event.subtitle: October 17, 2026
event.description: Nineteen sessions on making, learning, and finding a creative voice. Revisit the tenth-anniversary gathering through four connected themes.
event.markdown: Two keynotes, our first panel, sixteen workshops, and ten years of learning together. Collage together: a bright yellow p5.js canvas filled with names, words, shapes and the phrase "Collage together" that attendees added live at the end of Dan Shiffman's opening keynote, with an "Add yours" QR code in the corner. The shared collage at the end of Daniel Shiffman's opening keynote. ## Ten years in On October 17 we marked ten years of CC Fest. People joined from Sarajevo, Glasgow, Athens, Brighton, Minneapolis, the East Bay, Oregon, and elsewhere. Some were here for the first time; others had returned again and again. By my count, this was our thirtieth event. Since there is some confusion about the exact number I suggested in the chat that CC Fest is zero-indexed. The idea for CC Fest has stayed the same: a place to support creativity and learning, open and inclusive, where we learn together. Dan Shiffman hosted the first CC Fest at ITP, and Lauren Lee McCarthy's work on p5.js helped shape how many of us think about tools and community. Having them open and close the anniversary meant a lot to me. This year we added our first panel and joined the month's Processing Community Day celebrations. ## Why keep making? Dan opened with a question: if AI can write the code, why learn to write it? Drawing on Mitch Resnick, he described coding as a way to think and find a voice. Mistakes, exploration, and slowness were things he would not want to lose. > "The tedious stuff is the creative part." Daniel Shiffman He used Allison Parrish's collage metaphor to ask what disappears when a work's sources and processes are hidden. In the community he described, sketches and remixes circulate with their seams showing. He ended by inviting everyone to add to a shared p5.js canvas. The gathering itself became a collage. Explore these sessions - ## How do we make tools our own? Naoto Hieda explicitly picked up Dan's argument for taking time. In the Neocities workshop, that became a rhythm: edit one thing, save, reload, and look at what changed. Tristan Bunn offered another way into familiar ideas through his Python port of The Nature of Code. Presenting from Australia at 3:35 in the morning, he stayed after the talk to help a teacher get py5 running in VS Code. Caleb Foss approached the question through declarative code: describe the result you want instead of spelling out every step. Kemi Ukadike's playground asked makers to state an intention and a description before adding an object, preserving those decisions in a portable schema card. These were different ways to make a tool easier to understand, question, and shape. They also left room for different positions on AI: Kemi described practical access benefits from assistance, while Caleb explored alternatives to relying on large language models. Explore these sessions - - - - ## What can a few rules produce? Julien Gachadoat reconstructed John Roy's Segrid from its image and published process notes, then varied the rules to make new patterns. Sai Ram Ved Vijapurapu built a black-and-white ripple by giving similar shapes slightly different timing. In both workshops, a small change in a rule produced a visible change in the work. Matthew Raupp's Collage Machine brought chance into composition: a tool offered fragments, and a person decided how to arrange them. It echoed Dan's shared collage without using the same software. Kofi Oduro began further from the screen, asking people to combine a color and a meal, then imagine how the dish would move, sound, and smell. As his webcam became a grid of green-and-purple faces in Hydra, those private associations became starting points for play. Kofi Oduro's Hydra sketch: a webcam image pixelated, recolored in green and purple, and repeated in a grid of small tiles. Kofi Oduro's webcam, pixelated and tiled in Hydra. Explore these sessions - - - - ## What happens when code meets a material? Blair Subbaraman showed the same basket-weave design printed with different machines and materials. Sandra Soto raised her hand beside a servo-driven creature, connecting Teachable Machine, a micro:bit, and a motor. Aleksandra Jovanić worked out how a curve could leave one face of a printable cube net and arrive at the correct edge of another. Shane Curry held an LED grid beside the software that animated it. A material, a gesture, a fold, and a pattern of light each made a different part of the process visible. Sandra Soto raises her hand in front of a laptop camera, and a smiley-face creature mounted on a servo turns in response, wired to a micro:bit on her desk. Sandra Soto's hand beside the servo creature. Aleksandra Jovanić's final sketch: an unfolded cube net in which colored spline lines cross from face to face without breaking. Aleksandra Jovanić's curves cross the faces of a printable cube net. Missy Cooper brought that question back to a viewer's experience. After asking participants to find an object that "remembers a hand," she described a painting whose conductive border triggers a line of text. Should the line stay, fade, or vanish when a finger lifts? That was a storytelling decision. She asked people to connect an action, a response, and a reason in one sentence. > "The hard part is usually the because." Missy Cooper Missy Cooper's earlier screen-based piece: a p5.js sketch where viewers scratch away black paint over an illustration of two hands to reveal a story about the red thread of fate. Missy's earlier screen-based scratch-away piece. This year's workshop took the idea into a physical painting. Shane's use of coding agents alongside his opposition to visual generative AI, and Missy's discussion of AI as a useful rubber duck, kept the conversation open. The sessions did not arrive at one position on these tools. Explore these sessions - - - - - ## How do we learn by looking together? Emily Thomforde made a bouncing ball's behavior inspectable by plotting its height and velocity. Jessica Valarezo used invented basketball data to show what happens when a model trained on close shots encounters a different range of shots. Both moved beyond a plausible-looking result to ask what was happening underneath. M DeNardo let a Scratch demo fail and kept teaching. When two scripts shared the same arrow key, other eyes helped find the problem. On our first teaching panel, David DeLiema described the humor and care that can enter those debugging conversations. > "There's humor, there's joy, there's empathy. It's human interaction. It's human connection." David DeLiema Amy B. Woodman connected questions about taste and judgment to the balance of order and chaos in Aleksandra's existing Take a Spline for a Walk tutorial. Daniel Schneider argued that policy discussions too often leave out students' desire to create, while describing how AI helped his father build a website. Adrienne Gifford reported that almost none of her seventh graders chose an optional AI agent for an identity-based pixel art project. She suggested a future panel with students, and I would love to make that happen. I closed the panel by asking educators to use the agency they have in their classrooms: make room for skeptical voices, let people see how tools work, and build a community where students can help shape the process. Explore these sessions - - - - ## Who gets to take part? Lauren returned to the origins of p5.js, where community statements, accessibility, and rotating leadership were part of building the tool. Opening Captions, made with Alison O'Daniel through Social Software, treated the placement and appearance of captions as expressive choices. In the Q&A, she pointed to disability-community work such as Alt Text as Poetry and asked what we assume about the person receiving what we make. Speaking about participation in the p5.js community, she offered an invitation worth carrying into CC Fest's next ten years: > "You don't need to be an expert. You don't need to prove yourself before you get here." Lauren Lee McCarthy Explore these sessions - ## Thank you Thank you to Dan and Lauren; to Amy, Daniel, David, and Adrienne for trying something new with us; to every workshop presenter; and to everyone who joined. Francisca José Rodrigues co-hosted and designed the refreshed website. Shristi Singh, who has helped with CC Fest's design for years, built its new front-page interactives. Francisca also volunteering during the event and helped keep us on schedule. Thank you to them and to the volunteers who keep this gathering going. Every session has a recap and replay below. If you teach AP CS A, join us for [Visible Java: Processing for AP CS A](https://ccfest.rocks/events/visible-java/), a free online camp in November and December, with dates set from the interest list. We will be back in the spring.

sessions.title: Why keep making?
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Opening keynote — Daniel Shiffman
sessions.markdown:
Daniel Shiffman opened CC Fest's tenth anniversary by taking on the question he said he had been avoiding: if AI can write the code, why learn to write it? He framed his answer as a reflection on what he values in the creative coding community rather than a demonstration, and admitted he had put the talk together that morning.

He began with Allison Parrish's essay "Language Models Can Only Write Ransom Notes." Using Parrish's collage metaphor, he asked what disappears when the sources and processes behind a work are hidden. Shiffman contrasted that with the collage he sees in open source creative coding, where people share sketches, tutorials and remixes and the seams stay visible. CC Fest, which he hosted at ITP in its early years, was his example of that second kind of collage: people figuring out code together with a laptop and a question. He also wrote a short sketch about whether to count the anniversary as ten or eleven, since code counts from zero.

Drawing on Mitch Resnick's argument that coding is like writing, a way to think and find a voice, Shiffman recast the question as whether we want AI to do the thinking for us. He placed creative coding in a longer history of rule-based making, from Islamic geometric tilings to Inca quipu and Guna molas, and described how teaching a little physical computing to first-year students reminded him of the joy of a first working LED. Code, he argued, is a material too, and Parrish and Seymour Papert both point to sustained attention to that material as the source of meaningful work.

He named three things he would not want to lose to prompting: mistakes, exploration and slowness. A looping "whoops" video stood in for mistakes. Daily sketching practices by Zach Lieberman and others illustrated exploration, and his habit of writing one line, running it and then writing the next illustrated slowness. All three happen in the middle of a process, which he described as the part that is tedious and also the creative part. He added that AI can still be an interesting material to open up and critique, citing Maya Man's work, and said he plans to explore that in a spring course. The session ended with a quick participatory p5.js collage that attendees contributed to live.

## Three takeaways

- Ask what the learner should be doing, not only what the tool can do. Shiffman's reframe of "why learn to code?" as "do you want AI to do the thinking for you?" gives teachers a question to bring to students (00:15:01–00:16:20).
- Start with analog instructions. His opening exercise has students draw something, write instructions for it, and swap with a classmate to see what gets lost in translation (00:18:17–00:19:15).
- Protect the middle of the process. Mistakes, exploration and slowness are where style and understanding form; the tedious work "is the creative part" (00:21:37–00:27:00).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion, adapted from Shiffman's classroom opener: draw a simple picture in one minute, write instructions for it without showing the drawing, and hand the instructions to a partner. Compare the two drawings, then translate the clearer instructions into five lines of p5.js and run them one line at a time.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eCtOUBIkyyw)

Links shared in the session chat:

- [Allison Parrish](https://www.decontextualize.com/)
- [Mitch Resnick](https://web.media.mit.edu/~mres/)
- [Zach Lieberman](http://zach.li/)
- [Live collage sketch](https://collage-p5.netlify.app/)
- [Processing Community Day events](https://day.processing.org/)

sessions.title: Access Is the Interface
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Access Is the Interface: Coding in the Age of AI — Kemi Ukadike
sessions.markdown:
Kemi Ukadike started from a personal experience: an AI assistant she uses for speech typing once drafted and tried to act on an email she had not asked for. Several participants said in chat that something similar had happened to them. Her question for the workshop was how to keep control of code and intention when AI tools are part of the process, and her answer drew on digital accessibility practice. If code has to follow accessibility rules such as WCAG, she argued, it also has to say clearly what it is for and what it is allowed to do.

She demonstrated with a p5.js playground set in UMADA, an Afrofuturist storyworld she is building, set 200 years in the future. Children altered by a secret lab live in a garden that works like a Faraday cage, or a sandbox in coding terms: anything can be added, but nothing leaves without permission. Participants could place objects, including glyphs from a sign-based language she designed, using mouse, touch, words or face tracking. Before adding anything they had to state an intention and write a description, and they could choose whether an object moves.

Partway through, a participant asked what the schema card was. Ukadike explained that it grew out of moving her work between ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other tools and losing details each time. A schema card records each object's purpose, description, text alternative, controls and permissions, along with the code, so the requirements travel with the work. The playground lets participants download their own card.

The discussion turned to how she builds tools like this. Ukadike, who learned p5.js at ITP and worked as a journalist before that, described herself as a strong editor and said AI assistance lets her build accessible tools much faster, while still requiring her to check and debug what it produces. In response to a question about writing descriptions for creative work, she recommended starting simple, since you do not know who will encounter the work, and adding sophistication only where the work needs it.

## Three takeaways

- State intention in the code. Requiring a purpose and description before an object enters the sketch makes the work easier to review, for people and for AI tools (00:17:36–00:19:08).
- Keep requirements portable. A schema card holds accessibility and permission requirements alongside the code so they survive moves between tools and collaborators (00:22:54–00:25:59).
- Write descriptions for an unknown reader. Begin with the simplest accurate description and add complexity only when the work calls for it (00:47:06–00:50:14).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion: take a small p5.js sketch you already have and, before changing any code, write one sentence of intention and one plain description for each shape on the canvas. Then try the workshop playground and compare your notes with the schema card it generates.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X_0QIDMiMBU)

- [Access Is the Interface playground](https://ukadike.github.io/accessible-by-design-prototyping/access-agent-consent.html) (checked October 19; includes the printable field guide and schema card)
- [Accessible by Design](https://ukadike.github.io/accessible-by-design-prototyping/index.html)
- [Kemi Ukadike on GitHub](https://github.com/ukadike/ukadike)
- Further reading listed on the workshop page: WCAG 2.2; W3C, Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities; Hamraie and Fritsch, Crip Technoscience Manifesto; Costanza-Chock, Design Justice; NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

sessions.title: Making a portfolio on Neocities
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Making a portfolio on Neocities — Naoto Hieda
sessions.markdown:
Naoto Hieda ran a small, hands-on, beginner-friendly workshop on building a personal website with plain HTML on Neocities. Hieda's case for doing this rather than relying on Instagram was practical. A social feed limits you to images and captions, while your own page can hold hyperlinks, embedded maps and posts, and interactive p5.js sketches that visitors can actually use. They placed Neocities in a longer story of small, open corners of the web, from GeoCities to Glitch, which closed last year, as spaces where people can express themselves outside the boxes platforms impose.

Participants made free accounts, downloaded a template Hieda adapted from an existing Neocities HTML portfolio template, and dragged its files into their dashboards. To keep things casual, they built a cooking blog rather than an artist portfolio, and showed how the same structure works for showcasing creative work. Starting from index.html, they explained each step in plain terms: the page title that shows in the browser tab, paragraphs, headings as chapters, and unordered and ordered lists for ingredients and steps. The template injects a shared header and footer, so a site title changes in one place. Hieda kept the original template's credit in the footer and encouraged participants to credit what they remix.

Echoing Daniel Shiffman's keynote, they insisted on small steps: edit one thing, save, reload, and check, so that when something breaks you know where to look. They broke a tag on purpose to show what happens. When adding images, they covered habits that Instagram normally handles for you, such as resizing phone photos to about 1,000 pixels, choosing JPEG for photographs, and keeping file names simple. They also explained alt text for screen readers and noted that describing an image can be a creative choice. In the final minutes they embedded a p5.js sketch with the editor's iframe code, which they described as unlocking a lot for anyone who already makes sketches.

## Three takeaways

- Your own page can do what a feed cannot. Plain HTML can hold links, embeds and live, interactive sketches, not just images and captions (00:10:24–00:11:33).
- Edit, save, reload. Small steps make broken pages easy to diagnose, and breaking something on purpose is a good way to learn (00:26:20–00:28:49).
- Prepare images for the web. Resize photos, use JPEG for photographs, keep file names readable, and write alt text (00:37:45–00:45:23).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion: make a one-page site on Neocities for a single p5.js sketch. Add a heading, a short paragraph about how you made it, the sketch embedded with the editor's iframe code, and alt text for one still image. Save and reload after each change.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7cjI9mmIyY)

- [Neocities](https://neocities.org/)

sessions.title: Making Sense of Data with Live Visualization
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Making Sense of Data with Live Visualization — Emily Thomforde
sessions.markdown:
Emily Thomforde, a former computer science coordinator for the California Department of Education who now prepares new teachers, argued that creativity is not the first step. Before learners can make something with data, they need ways to make sense of it. She shared a set of free thinking routines, many adapted from Harvard's Project Zero, including Think, Feel, Care for empathy and Parts, Purposes, Complexities for systems. The focus of the session was one of her own: Min, Max, Middle. For any input or output, learners name the component, say whether it is an input or output, note the units (or that there are none), and then decide the minimum, maximum and typical everyday value. She noted that the newly rewritten CSTA standards say little about sensor data as input and output.

The coding moved from Scratch to Snap to p5.js. In Scratch she tied the cat's size to microphone loudness, then turned it into a live graph by moving the cat one step across the screen while setting its y position from loudness. Making the graph fill the screen meant scaling with multiplication and shifting with subtraction, which she connected to the sixth-grade standards on transformation. A pi simulation got the same treatment, so learners could see the estimate wander above and below the expected line instead of seeing only the final number. In Snap she showed min and max operators that record the true extremes, and left writing the minimum as an exercise.

For older students she offered a p5.js challenge: graph a bouncing ball's height over time. The map() function replaces the multiply-and-shift steps, and she pointed out that its arguments are the same questions Min, Max, Middle asks. Graphing the ball's velocity made the model's abrupt reversal at each bounce visible, even though the animation looked plausible to the eye. Daniel Schneider joined as navigator to graph Scratch face-size sensing live. In the closing Q&A, Thomforde said the biggest aha comes in physical computing, where knowing a sensor's range spares students from guessing numbers.

## Three takeaways

- Make sense of the numbers before creating with them. Min, Max, Middle gives learners a routine for any input or output: component, direction, units, minimum, maximum and typical value (00:06:04–00:09:57).
- Graph values over time. A live graph keeps the history of a variable, so learners can see how they got to a result and check it (00:13:21–00:23:12).
- Graphs can test a simulation. Plotting velocity showed a physics shortcut that looked right on screen but was not physically realistic (00:37:14–00:40:40).

## Try it

Adapted from Thomforde's Scratch demo: add the face-sensing extension, set the cat's y position to face size, and move it one step at a time with the pen down. Then adjust the scale and shift until the graph fills the stage, and record the minimum, maximum and middle values you observe.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=arvYvAOzrQ4)

- [Session navigation document with all project links](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IGF2V5PgZHwNOK4Bl_s5iEOtYTvHl5YR3d9j9gcYUpY/)

sessions.title: 3D printing with p5.fab!
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — 3D printing with p5.fab! — Blair Subbaraman
sessions.markdown:
Blair Subbaraman, finishing a PhD at the University of Washington, introduced p5.fab, a p5.js library he started several years ago for writing machine instructions directly instead of modeling objects. Participants came with a wide range of experience, from people who make generative shapes and plotter parts to teachers looking for ways to bring code and 3D printing to high school students.

He began with the usual workflow: design geometry in CAD, slice it into layers, and send the resulting G-code to the printer. That pipeline works, he said, but it separates geometry from settings and from the physical result, so every problem means a long trip back through the software. It is also hard to share, since a print depends on the machine, filament and calibration. Yet many failures are interesting. He showed prints from the "Cursed Benchies" community and work by artists who lean into the gap between digital plan and physical outcome, including filament sculptures generated with Processing, clay prints that pool where the printer pauses, and plotter drawings made with watercolor brushes that flex.

p5.fab skips the slicer. Most G-code is just "move in a straight line," with values for position, speed and how much material to extrude. In his browser editor, which needs no installation or printer, Subbaraman built up from moving to the center of the bed to extruding a line, a square and then stacked layers. He changed the extrusion multiplier the way you would change stroke weight in p5.js, adjusted speeds, and showed the G-code values change in response. Using circles whose diameter follows a sine wave, he grew a wavy vessel, then used map() to soften the curve so it could print without support. He showed the same basket-weave project printed in four materials, including homemade Play-Doh paste, and a remix graph on the site where people share settings that worked for them. A final video showed a MIDI controller changing print settings live as the machine ran.

In Q&A, participants asked about Bambu printers, pen plotters, Blender and AI tools. He described his PhD interviews about printer maintenance and his aim of helping people get to know their machines rather than tweaking settings in a slicer. One teacher planned to use the library to demystify printers for students, and another participant began writing a Bambu configuration during the session.

## Three takeaways

- G-code is approachable. Most of a print file is straight-line moves with position, speed and extrusion values, which you can write directly from code (00:09:43–00:16:01).
- Treat settings as creative material. Extrusion, speed and layer height can be varied within a print, the way stroke weight is in a sketch (00:24:16–00:33:50).
- Share settings, not just shapes. Because results depend on machine and material, sharing the code and settings that worked lets others adapt a print (00:44:04–00:45:00).

## Try it

Adapted from the workshop: open a new sketch in the copypastes editor, draw a stack of circles from z = 0 to 50, and set each circle's diameter to 40 + 5 × sin(t), where t maps z from 0 to 2π. Preview it, then download the G-code if you have a printer.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6kxCBhsPTmE)

- [p5.fab workshop materials](https://github.com/machineagency/p5.fab-workshop/)
- [copypastes editor](https://www.copypastes.xyz/sketch/new)
- [TRELLIS image-to-3D model](https://microsoft.github.io/TRELLIS/) (shared by a participant in response to a question; not a presenter resource)

sessions.title: The Nature of Code, but Python
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — The Nature of Code, but Python — Tristan Bunn
sessions.markdown:
Presenting from Australia at 3:35 in the morning, Tristan Bunn walked through his Python port of the second edition of Daniel Shiffman's The Nature of Code. His tagline was "Python wearing a Processing costume." He wanted the port to stay as close to the book as possible, so readers could follow each chapter, from random walks to neural networks, in Python instead of JavaScript.

The port is built on py5, Jim Schmitz's Python 3 library that runs on the Processing engine. Unlike the older [Processing.py](http://Processing.py), py5 can use the wider Python ecosystem, including NumPy, and can also load Processing's Java libraries. Bunn wrote a plugin for Thonny, a beginner Python editor that bundles its own interpreter and runs portably from a desktop or USB drive. With the plugin and recommended settings, Thonny looks and behaves much like the Processing editor. He likes py5's static mode for teaching because beginners can draw shapes before learning about setup and draw.

He sorted the translation work into three kinds. Much of it carried over line by line: size() instead of createCanvas(), snake\_case names such as mouse\_x, remap() because map is a Python built-in, and dimension-specific vector classes. Some logic had to be rethought. Multi-file sketches became modules, global variables need Python's global keyword, Matter.js gave way to Pymunk with a shared constants file to match its physics, toxiclibs ran directly as its original Java library, and ml5.js was replaced by scikit-learn, which trains the gesture classifier before the window opens. Finally, Python allowed simplifications he enjoys, such as operator overloading for vector math, comprehensions and slice notation. He said he finds math written in Python reads almost better than standard notation. He also pointed to Holly Grimm's separate port, which places the book's runnable examples in Jupyter notebooks.

The talk finished early, and Bunn stayed for an extended conversation with a high school teacher about running py5 in VS Code. The answer: create a virtual environment, pip install py5, which brings the Processing libraries with it, then run sketches from the terminal. py5 also needs Java 17 or newer. The Thonny plugin offers to download Java the first time it runs; outside Thonny, follow the Java steps in py5's [installation guide](https://py5coding.org/content/install.html).

## Three takeaways

- py5 brings Processing to Python 3. It runs on the Processing engine while opening up Python libraries such as NumPy and scikit-learn (00:07:57–00:10:01).
- Thonny with a py5 plugin offers a Processing-like starting point for beginners, with a bundled interpreter and no system install required (00:10:01–00:13:58).
- Porting is a design exercise. Some code translates line by line, some needs new logic, and some becomes simpler in the new language (00:14:55–00:25:34).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion: set up py5 (its documentation recommends Thonny with the py5 plugin for beginners), open the vectors chapter in the port repository, and rewrite one vector calculation from the p5.js version using operator overloading. Compare which version reads more like the math in the book.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D-kuxp1MJlI)

- [Nature of Code in py5 (port repository)](https://github.com/tabreturn/py5-nature-of-code), also linked from the Nature of Code website under Additional Resources
- [CC Fest talk materials and slides](https://github.com/tabreturn/cc-fest-noc-py5)
- [py5 documentation](https://py5coding.org/), including the [installation guide](https://py5coding.org/content/install.html)

sessions.title: Recoding: Tracing the origins of generative art
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Recoding: Tracing the origins of generative art — Julien Gachadoat
sessions.markdown:
Julien Gachadoat, a generative artist based in Bordeaux who works as v3ga, has used Processing for about 20 years and helped translate its early alpha version. His practice centers on autonomous systems drawn with pen plotters; he estimated he has made 700 to 800 plots over roughly seven years of near-daily iteration, a habit he linked to Zach Lieberman, whom Daniel Shiffman had cited in the keynote. He also showed a dice-based drawing protocol he first used with Vera Molnár in 2023, now installed so visitors can start their own plotted drawings.

The workshop centered on the ReCode Project, which Matthew Epler started in 2012 to publish code for pioneering computer art from the 1960s and 1970s. Its three goals were to bring that work back into circulation, offer a resource for practitioners and educators, and build a community. When Gachadoat went to use it for a workshop in Nantes earlier this year, the site was offline. With participants from that workshop, he rebuilt it in about two weeks, with some AI help, and relaunched it in the spring using p5.js. Most entries come from Computer Graphics and Art, a 1970s magazine edited by Grace Hertlein at Chico State, with scans preserved by the Compart archive. He noted that some artists, including Manfred Mohr, have asked that their work not be recoded, and the site respects that. A submission form is planned.

He then recoded John Roy's Segrid (1973) live in the p5.js editor. Reading the artist's published process notes alongside the image, he replaced the original ring-by-ring procedure with nested loops over a grid. Distance from the center, measured in concentric square rings, set how many lines each cell received. The key insight, which he said took him a while to find, was that each cell is one quarter-pattern rotated four times around its center. Letting lines run past the quarter created the interference patterns he finds most beautiful. With the grid at 17 by 17 and the right parameters, the original reappeared.

The last part turned the recode into a new system. He rotated by 45 degrees, scaled each cell with a sine of the frame count, and offset the phase by distance from the mouse, then mapped opacity to scale for a sense of depth. He said he still loves this moment at 51, and that looking at work from the 1970s often makes him feel he is reinventing the wheel.

## Three takeaways

- Recoding is a way to study history. Working out how a 1973 drawing was made, with punch cards and no screen preview, builds appreciation for the pioneers and their constraints (00:14:32–00:16:02).
- Look for the hidden symmetry. Segrid's pattern became simple once it was seen as one quarter rotated four times (00:31:06–00:42:06).
- A recode is a starting point. Small changes to rotation, time and mouse input turned a historical system into new work (00:45:16–00:55:03).

## Try it

Adapted from the workshop: open Gachadoat's Segrid sketch, change the rotation in the pattern loop from 90 to 45 degrees, then drive the number of lines per cell with sin(frameCount / 50). Pick one artwork from the ReCode Project and write down how you think it was made before reading its code.

sessions.title: La tecnología como lenguaje creativo
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — La tecnología como lenguaje creativo: de la IA al código, del código al mundo físico. — Sandra Soto
sessions.markdown:
Sandra Soto, an electronic artist and educator from Buenos Aires, led CC Fest's Spanish-language workshop. She came to technology through art and experimentation, and since 2012 has worked in schools as a technology facilitator, supporting teachers on projects and teaching children programming. She began with context: technology in schools needs more than tools. It starts with the community a school serves, then infrastructure such as the institutional accounts Buenos Aires schools use, then criteria for AI. She described a new annex to the city's guidance that introduces AI progressively, with a teacher mediating for younger students before older students learn with it directly.

She framed programming as a third language. Primary students are learning the structure of Spanish and also learning English, and then she arrives with a language that is neither, one that helps people communicate with machines. She shared a project she first presented at a CC Fest teacher camp, in which sixth graders aged 10 and 11 learned p5.js through a unit on data and stories: coordinates and the canvas, shapes and color, then movement, then loading text data to make a word cloud. With very simple code, students produced images and interactions that summarized the stories they had read.

Participants were then invited to build an interactive creature in p5.js from geometric shapes, starting from her example. Her prompts mirrored classroom moves: make it respond to mouseX and mouseY, and "break the rule" by changing a value in working code to see what happens. The final step took the creature off the screen. Using the Make: AI Robots site, she trained classes in Teachable Machine, linked them through a MakeCode example to a micro:bit, and added a servo. On camera, her physical creature responded to the two classes she had trained.

She closed with a reflection on "atarlo con alambre," an Argentine expression for making do and finding another way when materials run short, and a question echoing the keynote: if AI can write the code, what should we learn when we learn to code? Her answer was that students need prior knowledge and an understanding of AI's risks before they can work and talk with it. She is completing a master's thesis in electronic arts on links between textiles and the origins of computing.

## Three takeaways

- Treat code as a third language. Students learning Spanish and English at the same time can see programming as another language with its own syntax (00:13:21–00:14:37).
- Break the rule. Giving students working code and asking them to change one value is a low-risk way into understanding it (00:24:28–00:29:08).
- Move from screen to world in small steps. Teachable Machine, MakeCode and a micro:bit let a sketch-based idea become a physical creature without heavy electronics (00:29:08–00:35:13).

## Try it

Adapted from the workshop: draw a creature in p5.js using only circles, rectangles and lines. Make one part follow mouseX, then change one number in the code and describe what changed. If you have a micro:bit, follow the Make: AI Robots steps to trigger a movement from a Teachable Machine class.

## Watch and explore

sessions.title: A Painting, a Circuit, a Story
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — A Painting, a Circuit, a Story — Melissa Cooper
sessions.markdown:
Missy Cooper, a painter and creative technologist who has taught art and computer science, returned to CC Fest with a planning-first workshop on interactive art. Last year her participants virtually scratched away the surface of a painting to reveal the story beneath it. This year she took the artwork off the screen: a painting with conductive paint hidden in its black border, wired so that a touch reveals a line of text in a p5.js sketch. Instead of building the circuit live, she asked participants to plan, with only paper, a pen or their thoughts, and framed the hour as a game with levels. The question to carry throughout was what the interaction helps someone notice.

Level one was quiet looking. Participants spent 30 seconds with an object within reach that "remembers a hand" and then wrote what trace the hand had left. Their responses in chat included scissors whose gold finish had worn through where they were held, fingerprints on a phone, and an embroidery tin rubbed bare by three generations of women. Cooper's own object was a chair in her painting; touching its arm would reveal a line about a cushion holding a shape no one dared disturb.

Level two mapped the path from touch to sensor to board to message to story, with three ways in depending on budget: paper and copper tape, a Makey Makey that turns a touch into a key press, or an Arduino with capacitive sensing. The sketch follows three rules: a new touch reveals the story, the reveal button does the same, and reset returns to rest. The "boss level" was a bug she kept on purpose. Holding a finger on the paint restarted the reveal over and over, so the sentence never settled long enough to read. The fix, edge detection, reacts only at the moment touch changes. She then asked whether the line should stay, fade or vanish when the finger lifts. If AI wrote the sketch, she said, it would make that storytelling choice for you, and it is one worth keeping. She also said AI can be a useful rubber duck and can make making more equitable for people with different abilities.

Level three condensed each idea into one sentence: when someone does something, the work responds, because of a reason. "The hard part is usually the because," she said. She repeated the walkthrough for late arrivals and promised facilitator, student and circuit guides with the slides.

## Three takeaways

- Plan before building. One sentence, "when someone does this, the work responds, because…", can anchor an interactive piece, and the "because" is the hard part (00:25:47–00:28:37).
- React to the edge. If a held touch restarts an action, respond only when the input changes, not while it stays the same (00:20:09–00:23:06).
- Keep the storytelling choices. Whether text stays, fades or vanishes is an artistic decision, not a default (00:23:06–00:25:47).

## Try it

From the workshop: choose an object near you that has been shaped by hands. Spend 30 seconds looking at it, write one line about the trace the hand left, and finish the sentence "When someone touches it, \[response\] appears, because \[reason\]." Prototype the touch with a key press in p5.js before wiring anything.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u7Od8F-Xzk0)

sessions.title: Teaching Creativity Today
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Teaching Creativity Today — Amy B. Woodman, Daniel Schneider, David DeLiema, Adrienne Gifford
sessions.presenter: Amy B. Woodman, Daniel Schneider, David DeLiema & Adrienne Gifford
sessions.markdown:
CC Fest's first panel asked how to teach creativity through creative coding when AI can make almost anything. Amy B. Woodman, senior program manager at the Processing Foundation and a former classroom teacher, brought together three colleagues: Daniel Schneider, a former Tucson high school math and computer science teacher who has written middle school and AI curricula for [Code.org](http://Code.org) and now Hello World CS; David DeLiema, a learning scientist at the University of Minnesota who studies failure and play in learning; and Adrienne Gifford, in her 21st year teaching middle school computing and STEM and a collaborator with the University of Washington's Center for Learning, Computing, and Imagination. They had written questions for each other in advance without sharing answers, so the conversation unfolded like a podcast.

Woodman opened with her worry: making is how we learn to think, discover our tastes and preferences, learn to judge, and learn to express ourselves. If AI makes things for us, she asked, what happens to that? Schneider said that rooms where standards and policies are written now focus on technical skills, AI careers and even staying ahead of other countries, and that this narrative leaves out students' own desire to create. He argued that if self-expression is the goal, AI complicates the path but does not change the goal, and offered a counterpoint: his 70-year-old father used AI to finally build the quirky website no consultant understood.

DeLiema described debugging as full of open-ended, creative choices: what counts as wrong, what to blame, how to intervene, and what you want to learn from the moment. "There's humor, there's joy, there's empathy. It's human interaction. It's human connection," he said of the conversations around broken code. He described students who sang to each other when something failed and worried about handing that social process to a tool. Pointing to Courtney Cazden's research on prompts, he noted that a hint only works if you already have the knowledge it cues, which is why learners have to own their learning process.

Gifford reported that her seventh graders made identity-based pixel art in Python with an optional AI agent, and almost none chose to use it. In reflections, they said they wanted their work to be authentic, that their ideas were better than AI's, that they preferred help from teachers and peers, and that they had concerns about artists' work and water use. Twelve-year-olds, she said, are asking the same questions as artists and researchers, and students should be able to question, change or reject the tools. What they want protected is agency over their creative process, not speed. She suggested next year's panel feature students.

Woodman described the Art + Code curriculum for art teachers, guided by Seymour Papert's idea that educators create conditions for invention rather than provide ready-made knowledge. Tutorials such as Build a World and a shared Drawing Tool give learners challenges just out of reach, results that are clearly their own, and communal moments where they use each other's work. She also cited the balance of order and chaos in Aleksandra Jovanić's existing Take a Spline for a Walk tutorial, connecting constraints in a drawing system to the judgment a maker develops. Saber Khan closed by urging teachers to make their classrooms places where skeptical voices are heard.

## Three takeaways

- Ask the students. Gifford's seventh graders mostly declined an optional AI helper, citing authenticity, their own ideas, human help and ethics (00:14:58–00:18:28).
- Debugging is creative and social. Noticing, blaming and fixing are open-ended choices, and the talk around them builds connection (00:10:00–00:13:50).
- Design challenges just out of reach. Papert's "conditions for invention" guided tutorials where every learner's result is different and shared (00:19:24–00:24:52).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion, adapted from Gifford's classroom: on your next creative coding project, make an AI helper optional and ask students to write a short reflection on whether and why they used it. Share what they say with them, and with colleagues.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ria5PMpw8RQ)

- [Art + Code curriculum class on OpenProcessing](https://openprocessing.org/class/99495) (link shared in chat by Saber Khan)
- Panelist bios are on the CC Fest website.

sessions.title: Research-Paper-Monster-Mash
sessions.markdown:
Shane Curry is a professional traditional animator and the timing supervisor on American Dad, with credits that include She-Ra, Trolls, Duncanville and Golden Axe. He opened by explaining his specialty, the exposure sheet: a frame-by-frame chart of which drawings appear when, aligned to dialogue and camera moves. He described it as a static abstraction of real-time behavior among interdependent objects, even declaring camera moves at the top "like declaring variables."

His relationship with software has been uneasy. Every tool he loved, from Toon Boom Harmony to Blender and Unreal Engine, eventually left him behind as updates piled up, and he found that his successes came from working around software rather than with it. Over the past six months, agentic coding changed that. Working nights and weekends, he used AI coding agents to recreate experiments from as many research papers in his field as he could find. The process was creatively fulfilling and also made him ambivalent, given how endless the exploration became. It led him to a working definition: self-expression is the authored arrangement of data.

He showed what that means with lines. Strictly, a line is two points plus decisions about how much data to store between them. One input tracker is quick and honest in the moment but cuts corners when you draw fast; a smoothed version is honest after the fact but lags behind your hand. Artists, he argued, should be able to choose either on purpose, not get one by accident. He kept experiments small enough to debug what the agents were doing, using a chunky 4×3 pixel font for that reason, and explored subpixel animation on an 8×8 LED grid and an "animated codec," a QR-code-like cartoon that encodes a short animation in its own trembling lines. He built the slide software for the talk himself and drew its artwork by hand.

In a long Q&A, Curry explained that he searches for papers with code, judges them by whether the result excites him, and often learns from the agent that he has independently rediscovered published work. Asked about the animation industry, he said he is still exclusively a traditional animator, that few new shows are starting, and that he has more fun building tools than wrestling with large 3D packages. He remains against visual generative AI, which he sees as a finished product he cannot manipulate, but expects studios may one day build their own software for each production. His advice drew on a clothing metaphor: not everyone needs to make their own clothes, but everyone should learn to dress themselves.

## Three takeaways

- Expression lives in data decisions. How often a tool samples a stroke, and whether it smooths it, shapes what an artist can do (00:10:03–00:11:19).
- Keep experiments small enough to check. Simple, chunky systems made it possible to verify what coding agents were building (00:12:28–00:13:37).
- Choose real constraints. Arbitrary limits feel false, but your own domain expertise, and even your ignorance in a new field, can guide what you build (00:23:00–00:25:38).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion based on Curry's line demo: write two p5.js drawing tools, one that draws a line between raw mouse positions each frame and one that eases toward the mouse with lerp(). Draw quickly with each and decide which kind of honesty you want.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ifdT65Gg-Is)

sessions.title: Machine Learning in Motion
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Machine Learning in Motion: Designing Better Technology for Athletes — Jessica Valarezo
sessions.markdown:
Jessica Valarezo, a former computer science teacher now working as an engineer at an education technology company, led a small, interactive session on how machine learning is used in sports, with attention to gaps between men's and women's athletics. Participants rated themselves around 2 out of 5 on machine learning, so she tailored the hour to fundamentals, using a set of browser simulations she built (with AI assistance and many rounds of revision) and shared as a single website.

She laid out a sequence: data becomes inputs, inputs go to a model, the model produces an output, and people make decisions with that output. In a shot explorer trained on invented basketball shots, participants moved a shooter and defender to find the hardest and easiest shots; the model agreed with intuition that distance and a close defender make shots harder. An animation showed training as fitting a line to reduce error, and a 3D view showed the search for a low point on an error surface.

In the coding section, participants changed a small logistic regression model and predicted the effect before retraining. Removing the defender input lowered test accuracy from 73 percent. Training only on close shots made accuracy collapse to roughly a coin flip on longer shots the model had never seen, which she connected to the question of who is in the data and who is missing. A clip from a dramatic late-game moment in this year's NBA Finals, a game models had given long odds, prompted her to ask whether we even want a model to capture what made it thrilling.

Further simulations used pose estimation of landings, where a hidden knee lowers the model's confidence, and an injury-risk curve inspired by FC Barcelona research, where participants debated where to set an alert threshold. Valarezo then examined claims from published studies. One women's football study showed improved knee mechanics after a program but did not track injuries or use a randomized comparison, so it could not show that the technology helped. A good prediction, she said, is not proof that a tool helps athletes. Women's teams often face different schedules, travel and resources, and she cautioned against offering technology as a quick fix where more trained experts are the real need, drawing a parallel to classrooms where a tool can stand in for a well-resourced teacher.

## Three takeaways

- Follow the chain from data to decision. Data, inputs, model, output and decision each involve choices about who benefits (00:06:28–00:09:06).
- Missing data breaks models. Training only on close shots left the model guessing on long ones, a reminder to ask whose data is included (00:21:33–00:24:00, 00:47:00–00:49:18).
- A good prediction is not proof of help. Claims that a tool helps athletes need outcomes such as injury rates and fair comparisons (00:42:34–00:46:00).

## Try it

From the workshop site: open the coding lab, write down a prediction, remove one input, and retrain. Then try the "close shots only" data and compare test accuracy. Discuss what a similar gap would mean for a model trained mostly on men's games.

## Watch and explore

sessions.title: Collage Machine, an Algorithmic Approach to Play
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Collage Machine, an Algorithmic Approach to Play — Matthew Raupp
sessions.markdown:
Matthew Raupp, an associate professor of UX design at the College for Creative Studies in Detroit and a member of Creative Coding Detroit, ran a hands-on workshop with Collage Machine, a Processing tool he has developed over several years for his art practice and his classes. It aims to balance artistic control and chance, and needs no coding experience. His path to creative code ran from a Commodore VIC-20 through Macromedia Director, Flash and ActionScript to Processing and p5.js.

Collage Machine began with early sketches that loaded a random photo on each click, then placed images randomly within the canvas, then made them draggable. The current version is the 36th. It began fully hand-coded, and in later versions he worked with ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude in a back-and-forth where he stays the author, asks the assistant to explain anything he does not understand, and builds in small increments. Conceptually he draws on Dada and Fluxus, which embraced chance, instructions and found material, and on contemporary collage artists and designers who build their own tools. He wants students to be tool builders, not only tool users.

The tool pulls from three folders of public domain material he has collected: objects, word fragments and graphics. Each button adds a random item at a random position and size. Participants then drag, scale, rotate, duplicate and delete, and can add colored shapes that blend in multiply mode. A dice button adds one of each type plus a color. His favorite controls randomly reposition and rescale selected pieces, which can turn a carefully arranged composition into a fresh starting point. There is no undo. Students ask for it, but he said it is hard to build and asks them to embrace what they are given. Several participants agreed with that choice, and many shared their compositions in chat as the session went on.

Raupp then thought aloud through a composition the way he does in class: placing a focal object on the rule of thirds, clustering and duplicating, finding shared shapes and sight lines, pushing scale to extremes, letting elements bleed off the edge, activating negative space and reading for hierarchy. In his sophomore design semiotics course, students load their own images, after first working in Photoshop, Illustrator and paper collage. He uses the tool to discuss how every tool shapes its outcomes, and how a library of images reflects its collector's lens. Asked about authorship and loss of control, he said the class reads and discusses both, and that he hopes to let the tool pull images from online sources in the future.

## Three takeaways

- Build tools, not just use them. A custom tool lets an artist set the constraints that shape their work, and makes visible how every tool shapes outcomes (00:20:22–00:21:40, 00:57:00–00:58:35).
- Mix control and chance. Random placement, the dice and reposition-and-rescale controls offer new starting points that the artist can then refine (00:35:34–00:39:30).
- Name the composition strategies. Rule of thirds, clustering, duplication, scale, bleed, focal point and hierarchy give students a vocabulary for what they are seeing (00:43:33–00:49:37).

## Try it

From the workshop: download Collage Machine, replace the objects folder with ten of your own photos, and make three compositions. For each, press P and S several times and save one variation you would not have made by hand. Write one sentence on what the randomness changed.

sessions.title: Delightful motion loops
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Delightful motion loops — Sai Ram Ved Vijapurapu
sessions.markdown:
Sai Ram Ved Vijapurapu has taken part in Genuary, a January challenge that offers a new generative art prompt each day, for several years. His sketches focus on motion rather than color or form: how to make things move in ways that feel satisfying. In this follow-along workshop he rebuilt one of last year's pieces, a stack of black and white shapes whose motion is driven by trigonometric functions, from an empty p5.js sketch.

He started with habits he uses in most sketches: a full-window canvas, sizes defined relative to the canvas width, and translate() to move the origin to the center so the x and y arguments stay free for motion. frameCount supplied a steadily increasing number, and the graphing calculator Desmos showed how sin() turns that number into a smooth wave between −1 and 1. Because that range is only a pixel or two, he used map() to stretch it to a quarter of the canvas height and slowed the input by multiplying frameCount by 0.1.

A loop drew many circles, largest first so each smaller one sits on top, alternating black and white using the remainder of the loop index divided by 2. Subtracting a small multiple of the loop index from each circle's input made each one lag slightly behind the next, producing a rippling pattern from about 20 lines of code. He then turned to the 12 principles of animation from Disney animators, using a circle-based visualization of them, and focused on easing: real objects speed up and slow down, as in the windup and release of a throw. A pure sine wave is smooth but plain. Experimenting in Desmos, he nested functions to reshape the motion, landing on atan(10 × sin(x)), which lingers at each end and moves quickly through the middle. Graphing first showed him the new minimum and maximum to use in map().

To finish, he made a perfect loop. Since sine repeats every 2π, setting the input to TWO\_PI × frameCount ÷ 120 completes one cycle in exactly 120 frames, and saveGif() with frame units records just that cycle. Swapping circles for squares with rectMode(CENTER) recreated the original piece. He encouraged everyone to try Genuary, saying that a daily practice and his own black-and-white constraint had helped him develop a recognizable style, echoing Daniel Shiffman's keynote.

## Three takeaways

- Graph before you code. Desmos makes it easy to see how a function behaves and what its range is before mapping it to motion (00:09:25–00:11:00, 00:31:11–00:36:46).
- Small offsets make rich patterns. Subtracting a little of the loop index from each shape's input creates lagging waves (00:22:22–00:26:30).
- Plan the loop length. Tie the input to TWO\_PI divided by a frame count so the animation repeats exactly, then save that many frames (00:41:11–00:49:00).

## Try it

From the workshop: in p5.js, draw ten nested circles whose y position is map(sin(x − i × 0.1), −1, 1, −height/4, height/4). Replace sin(x) with atan(10 × sin(x)), find its new range in Desmos, and update map(). Then set x to TWO\_PI × frameCount / 120 and record one 120-frame loop with saveGif('loop', 120, \{ units: 'frames' \}).

## Watch and explore

sessions.title: Livecoding with Scratch
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Livecoding with Scratch — M DeNardo
sessions.markdown:
M DeNardo has taught children ages 7 to 10 for about 20 years, often by live coding in front of them. Their session looked at live coding in Scratch both as a teaching method and as a way to show children how to generate ideas. They described live coding in a classroom as risky, a performance that takes practice and a certain athleticism, and best done in a framework where you can make something surprising quickly. Children, they said, want to see something special fast, so a full game is often the wrong scale for a first project.

Starting from a blank project, DeNardo built a forever loop that slowly grew a tiny Scratch cat while increasing its mosaic effect, then duplicated the sprite with a whirl effect. The overlapping effects produced a moiré pattern, which they pointed out could lead to a conversation about math and physics, not only coding. An attempt to recreate turtle-style move-and-turn shapes did not work, and they let it go on screen: when something fails, you keep teaching. Clones were their reliable fallback. A sprite that follows the mouse and clones itself every frame quickly fills the stage, and tying its size to the mouse's x position, then adjusting the scaling, gave the class a concrete way to talk about coordinates and inputs. Kids love it, they said, when you don't have it together and then pull off a magic trick.

Later demos added a variable-driven repeat loop, a pixelated background layer of randomly placed clones, and keyboard controls for the fisheye effect. They briefly showed Hydra, a browser live coding environment, to compare how other tools randomize values. When the arrow keys did nothing, a participant spotted that both scripts used the up arrow, which DeNardo turned into advice: trust the other eyes in the room, because a student will often see the bug first.

In the final minutes, a sixth-grade teacher asked about broadcast and custom blocks, which his students find difficult. DeNardo built a sprite that follows the mouse and broadcasts a message to change the backdrop when it touches the edge, debugged it live, and showed how the same behavior can become a custom block. They suggested naming messages explicitly and avoiding extra machinery that a project does not need.

## Three takeaways

- Start small and surprising. A forever loop with a growing effect gets children to a "wow" faster than a game (00:11:23–00:15:30).
- Model recovery. Dropping a demo that is not working, and saying so, shows students how to keep going (00:20:18–00:24:38).
- Let the room debug. Students often spot the mistake before the teacher, as with two scripts that both used the up arrow (00:47:54–00:49:46).

## Try it

Adapted from the session: in Scratch, make a sprite go to the mouse pointer forever and create a clone of itself each time. Change its size by mouse x divided by different numbers until the motion feels right, and talk through what x is doing.

## Watch and explore

Replay: [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wNq_k_fWk4)

- [Scratch](https://scratch.mit.edu/)

sessions.title: Improv Digitally, Sensorial and with Self Awareness
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Improv Digitally, Sensorial and with Self Awareness — Kofi Oduro (Illestpreacha)
sessions.markdown:
Kofi Oduro, a Montreal-based creative coder known as Illestpreacha, has kept a daily creative practice for almost seven years and has presented at CC Fest several times. The session grew out of work he did for recreational therapy. His starting point was that we live surrounded by inputs from social media and daily life, yet rarely notice that our senses, including smell, texture and temperature, are how we make sense of the world. He wanted participants to bring that awareness into code.

He began with "coding in your head." Participants named their fifth favorite color and seventh favorite meal, then merged the two. The chat filled with combinations such as polka dot peanut butter and jelly, white loaded nachos, red fried noodles and pink rice with chicken kebab. He then asked about texture and sound: are you crunchy, velvety, soggy? Would you hurt someone who stepped on you? These were questions, he noted, that an AI could not answer for you, because each person makes their own associations. Later he searched for a "fifth favorite meal" and showed that the generated answer fell back on the most common foods.

Next he turned those imagined dishes loose in live code. In Hydra, a few lines pixelated his webcam feed and ran it through a colorama effect, and he asked participants how their dish would move through the room, where it would land and how it would smell. As he shifted hues, participants described the image as fresh and citrusy, then icy like Montreal, then like plankton when he tiled his face 100 and then 225 times. Live Code Lab added a bouncing shape and simple sounds, and LocoMotion, a live coding language with motion-captured 3D dancers (and raccoons), showed how lighting and movement can push a scene toward a genre. A Halloween piece combining Sonic Pi, LocoMotion and Hydra showed how texture, motion and sound can create a mood without anything literally frightening on screen. Participants also offered the third song they would play on a rainy day, which he wove into an interactive fiction demo in Twine.

Asked about his process, he described a daily practice where a minute counts as much as an hour, weekly prompts and challenges for inspiration, sharing work in progress, and treating failure as part of the work. He urged adults to play more and to join more than one community, because people are eager to share what they love.

## Three takeaways

- Code in your head first. Combining unusual prompts gives each person associations no tool can supply (00:06:33–00:11:39).
- Short code can be expressive. Two or three lines of Hydra turned a webcam into a shared sensory experience (00:13:03–00:22:07).
- Consistency can be small. A daily practice where one minute counts, fed by prompts and communities, keeps ideas moving (00:49:11–00:55:00).

## Try it

From the workshop: write down your fifth favorite color and seventh favorite meal, merge them into one thing, and describe its texture, sound and smell. Then open Hydra, start from the camera, and change colors and repetition until the screen feels like your description.

sessions.title: Take a spline for a walk
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Take a spline for a walk — Aleksandra Jovanić
sessions.markdown:
Aleksandra Jovanić, a professor at the Faculty of Fine Arts of the University of Arts in Belgrade who teaches creative coding and physical computing, returned to CC Fest for the third time. Her session grew from an artist tutorial she made for the Processing Foundation on the spline functions introduced in p5.js 2.0, an implementation of Catmull-Rom curves that connect smoothly without the extra control-point bookkeeping the older curve functions required. The second part of that commission was an artwork, also called Take a Spline for a Walk.

She placed the project in a line of her earlier work about what happens at an edge: a book onto which generative output is projected so every page turn shows a new variation, an interest in Myriorama picture cards that join seamlessly in any order, and plotted globes whose lines cross from face to face without a visible break. For this project she wanted lines that leave one page of a folded eight-page zine and continue on the correct next page, and she then animated them. She admitted, with a meme, that she had overestimated how much she could show in one session, so she walked through finished, working code in OpenProcessing's tutorial mode rather than coding from scratch.

The steps built up gradually. First, a single square page, with each point stored as a page number plus relative coordinates and edges numbered clockwise from the top. Next, lines enter from one edge and leave by a different edge, filtering out the current edge so a line never exits where it entered. Then a choice familiar from early Processing lessons: bounce off the edge or wrap around to the opposite side. With two pages joined like the front and back of a sheet, lines flip and change edges as they cross. She constrains random positions to roughly 0.2–0.8 along an edge so thick lines never hit a corner, where they could continue onto two different faces.

Swapping straight lines for splines produced continuous curves, though with visible bends at the edges. For her globes she prefers Bézier curves, adding a tangent perpendicular to each edge so a line can cross smoothly. The final sketch draws a cube net in which every line continues correctly across all six faces, using a connection table that records, for each page and edge, which page comes next and how positions flip. It includes glue flaps so the result can be printed, folded and assembled. She said she had not found a general rule for other solids and that an AI chat tool had only restated her own approach, so she invited participants to fork the code and try other shapes.

## Three takeaways

- Splines connect smoothly by design. In p5.js 2.0, spline functions let curve segments join continuously without the old bookkeeping for first and last control points (00:04:55–00:08:08, 00:43:32–00:47:01).
- Edges are design decisions. Bounce, wrap or continue onto another face; each choice needs explicit rules, especially when moving to paper or 3D (00:29:33–00:39:00).
- Choose the curve for the join. Splines bend at page edges, while Béziers with tangents perpendicular to the edge let lines cross without a visible break (00:47:01–00:53:11).

## Try it

From the session: fork Jovanić's OpenProcessing tutorial, print the cube net, fold it and check that every line continues. Then change the random range along each edge from 0.2–0.8 to 0–1 and thicken the stroke to see why corners cause trouble.

## Watch and explore

sessions.title: Declare Independence (from LLMs)
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Declare Independence (from LLMs) — Caleb Foss
sessions.markdown:
Caleb Foss teaches web development at a community college in Joliet, near Chicago, and has taught game design, physical computing and virtual reality. Their title nodded to Björk, and their aim was to lower barriers and intimidation for artists and designers learning code. They said they usually cherish days when AI is not mentioned but found the day's conversations about it unusually thoughtful.

Foss began with instructions as art. Yoko Ono's Painting to Be Stepped On is a written score anyone can enact, and Sol LeWitt's wall drawings describe a process in which each person copies the wavering line above, so small variations build into a pattern. Both resemble a prompt in some ways, so Foss asked how prompting a large language model differs. One participant, who prompts as an artist, said they iterate on a single prompt to study a model's particular character, almost like a documentary photographer. Foss added environmental cost, the loss of human variation in the enactment, and the ideologies hidden in training data too large for anyone to know. Having studied machine learning a decade ago, when artists trained models on their own datasets, they described a sense of loss as the field moved to huge pre-trained models.

Their alternative was a shift from imperative code, which spells out the steps like a recipe, to declarative code, which describes the result. Foss noticed that students describe their ideas declaratively ("I want this on the screen, and when you click it, this happens"), and that translating those descriptions into steps can be both rewarding and a barrier. Declarative code lets the creator focus on the result while keeping full control. A-Frame, an established library, builds 3D and VR scenes from HTML tags whose attributes name position, rotation and color, and its built-in inspector lets learners adjust a scene and paste the changes back into code.

Foss then showed WebSpinner, a beginner-oriented library they have developed on and off for about five years. It offers custom HTML elements and a JavaScript interface for a 2D canvas, and it attaches properties such as anchor, angle, fill, velocity and origin directly to each shape, rather than transforming the whole canvas as p5.js does with push, translate and rotate. It uses full words instead of abbreviations, labeled values and the browser's accessibility features. Nesting one element inside another makes it inherit movement. A shape can respond to its own clicks without manual hit testing, and each new shape appears as an element in the browser's developer tools, where it can be edited live without the learner needing arrays. Foss invited collaborators, especially for documentation.

## Three takeaways

- Prompts and scores differ. Comparing LLM prompts with Ono's and LeWitt's instructions raises questions about variation, cost and whose values fill the gaps (00:09:35–00:18:00).
- Students often think declaratively. Code that describes the result can be a gentler entry point while keeping full creative control (00:18:00–00:21:00, 00:33:36–00:37:37).
- Attach properties to things. In A-Frame and WebSpinner, position, color and motion live on the object itself, which makes them easy to find and change (00:21:00–00:27:51, 00:40:24–00:47:22).

## Try it

Editorial suggestion: write a one-paragraph description of a simple scene, then build it twice, once in A-Frame as tags with attributes and once in p5.js as a sequence of steps. Compare which version was easier to change.

sessions.title: Who gets to take part?
sessions.source_title: Oct 17 recap — Closing keynote — Lauren Lee McCarthy
sessions.markdown:
Lauren Lee McCarthy closed CC Fest’s anniversary gathering by connecting the origins of p5.js with a broader question: how can people shape their relationships with technology? Her account of starting p5.js emphasized uncertainty, collective learning, and participation. The project began with questions about bringing Processing to the web and widening who could contribute. Community statements, accessibility, and rotating leadership were part of the work of building the tool.

> "You don't need to be an expert. You don't need to prove yourself before you get here." Lauren Lee McCarthy, on participation in the p5.js community

That approach continued in her discussion of Social Software, the UCLA lab she co-founded with Casey Reas. She described software as a social and cultural practice, with room for artists, students, and people outside technical fields to help decide what tools should do. Opening Captions, developed with Alison O’Daniel, offered a concrete example: caption placement and styling can become expressive parts of a film.

McCarthy then turned to participatory artworks that make technological relationships tangible. In her human-assistant performance, she inhabited the role of a home automation system, exposing tensions between convenience, intimacy, privacy, and control. A saliva-exchange project invited people to set terms for sharing intimate biological material, making questions of data ownership physical. A vehicle project used collective singing and changing prompts to explore the experience of automation and giving up control.

The discussion returned to teaching and access. McCarthy described conversations with students as a source of energy and possibility, and pointed toward accessibility practices as ways to reconsider communication itself. Her closing invitation was to remain makers: people who bring their own values into tools and systems, and who can question the futures those systems imply.

## Three takeaways

- An open tool also needs practices that invite people to participate: 00:04:04–00:08:21.
- Interfaces encode choices about relationships and control; participatory artworks can help people examine those choices: 00:12:03–00:25:45.
- Accessibility can shape artistic expression and provoke new questions about communication: 00:30:12–00:32:39.

## Try it

Editorial suggestion: choose a familiar interface and list what it assumes about its users. Sketch one change that gives people more control or more ways to participate.
